prompt:
There are 5 girls in a tennis class.

**How many different doubles teams of 2 girls each can be formed from the students in the class?**

solutions.title: Count teams for each girl, then fix double counting
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Call the girls A, B, C, D, E.
- Each girl can team up with any of the other 4 girls, so each girl is on 4 teams.
- $5 \times 4 = 20$ — but every team was counted twice (team BC was counted once for B and once for C).
- So there are $20 \div 2 = 10$ teams.

**Answer: 10 teams**

solutions.title: List them in order
solutions.body:
Write each team with the earlier letter first, so no team is repeated:

- With A: AB, AC, AD, AE → 4
- With B (not A): BC, BD, BE → 3
- With C: CD, CE → 2
- With D: DE → 1

$4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$

**Answer: 10 teams**

prompt:
The letters in MATH and OLYMPIADS are cycled separately as shown and placed in a numbered list (each row moves the first letter of each word to the end). The next correct spelling of both words MATH and OLYMPIADS will appear in row number $n$.

**Find the value of $n$.**

solutions.title: Find each cycle, then use the LCM
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- MATH has 4 letters, so it is spelled correctly every 4th row: rows 1, 5, 9, 13, …
- OLYMPIADS has 9 letters, so it is correct every 9th row: rows 1, 10, 19, 28, …
- Both are correct together every LCM(4, 9) = 36 rows.
- Starting from row 1, the next time is row $1 + 36 = 37$.

**Answer: $n = 37$**

solutions.title: Check the lists
solutions.body:
- MATH is correct in rows that are 1 more than a multiple of 4: 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29, 33, **37**, …
- OLYMPIADS is correct in rows that are 1 more than a multiple of 9: 1, 10, 19, 28, **37**, …
- The first row after row 1 that is in both lists is 37.

**Answer: $n = 37$**

prompt:
When two people shake hands with one another, that counts as one "handshake." Every person in a room shakes hands with each other person in the room exactly once. There are a total of 15 "handshakes".

**How many people are in the room?**

solutions.title: Each handshake is counted twice
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- If there are $n$ people, each shakes hands with $n - 1$ others. That gives $n \times (n-1)$, but every handshake gets counted twice (once by each person).
- So handshakes $= n \times (n - 1) \div 2$.
- We need $n \times (n-1) \div 2 = 15$, so $n \times (n - 1) = 30$.
- 30 is the product of two consecutive numbers: $6 \times 5$. So $n = 6$.

**Answer: 6 people**

solutions.title: Add people one at a time
solutions.body:
Each new person who walks in shakes hands with everyone already there:

| People | New handshakes | Total |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | 2 | 3 |
| 4 | 3 | 6 |
| 5 | 4 | 10 |
| 6 | 5 | **15** |

**Answer: 6 people**

prompt:
Boris and Natasha start at the same place and at the same time on a 200 meter circular track and run in the same direction. Boris runs at 5 meters per second and Natasha runs at 3 meters per second.

**How many meters has Natasha run when they first meet after starting?**

solutions.title: Boris must gain one full lap
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- They run the same direction, so they meet again when Boris has run exactly one lap (200 m) more than Natasha.
- Each second Boris gains $5 - 3 = 2$ meters.
- To gain 200 m takes $200 \div 2 = 100$ seconds.
- In 100 seconds Natasha runs $3 \times 100 = 300$ meters.

**Answer: 300 meters**

solutions.title: Make a table
solutions.body:
Track how far each has run and the gap between them:

| Time (s) | Boris (m) | Natasha (m) | Gap (m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25 | 125 | 75 | 50 |
| 50 | 250 | 150 | 100 |
| 75 | 375 | 225 | 150 |
| 100 | 500 | 300 | **200** |

A gap of 200 m (one whole lap) means Boris has caught Natasha. She has run 300 m.

**Answer: 300 meters**

prompt:
Maxie lies on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays, while he tells the truth on all other days. Minnie lies on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays, but she is truthful on all other days.

**On what day of the week could they both say, "Tomorrow, I will lie."?**

solutions.title: Look for a change from today to tomorrow
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- If a truth-teller says "Tomorrow I will lie," then tomorrow they really do lie.
- If a liar says it, it is false, so tomorrow they tell the truth.
- Either way, the statement can only be said on a day when the person's truth-telling **changes** from today to tomorrow.

| | Sun | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maxie | lie | truth | truth | truth | truth | lie | lie |
| Minnie | truth | truth | lie | lie | lie | truth | truth |

- Maxie changes Thu→Fri and Sun→Mon.
- Minnie changes Mon→Tue and Thu→Fri.
- Both change only from **Thursday** to Friday.

**Answer: Thursday**

solutions.title: Test each day
solutions.body:
Check each day: does the sentence work for both?

- **Monday:** Maxie tells truth; tomorrow (Tue) he tells truth, so "I will lie" would be false — but he is truthful. ✗
- **Tuesday, Wednesday:** Maxie truthful, but he doesn't lie the next day. ✗
- **Thursday:** Maxie is truthful and does lie on Friday ✓. Minnie lies on Thursday, so her statement must be false — and indeed she tells the truth on Friday ✓.
- **Friday, Saturday:** Maxie lies, but he also lies the next day (Sat/Sun), so his statement would be true. ✗
- **Sunday:** Maxie lies and tells truth Monday ✓, but Minnie is truthful Sunday and also truthful Monday, so her statement would be false. ✗

**Answer: Thursday**

prompt:
The price of a candy bar has increased 20%.

**How many candy bars can now be purchased for the amount of money that used to buy 42 candy bars?**

solutions.title: Turn the percent into a fraction
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- A 20% increase means a bar that cost 5¢ now costs 6¢. The new price is $\frac{6}{5}$ of the old price.
- So the same money buys only $\frac{5}{6}$ as many bars.
- $\frac{5}{6}$ of 42 is $42 \div 6 \times 5 = 35$.

**Answer: 35 candy bars**

solutions.title: Pick a nice price
solutions.body:
- Suppose a bar used to cost \$1.00. Then 42 bars cost \$42.
- After a 20% increase, a bar costs \$1.20.
- \$42 ÷ \$1.20 = 420 ÷ 12 = **35** bars.

**Answer: 35 candy bars**

prompt:
Six girls of differing heights are arranged in 2 rows of 3 each, as in the picture. Each girl is taller than the girl in front of her and also taller than the girl to her right.

**How many arrangements of the six girls are possible?**

solutions.title: List the arrangements systematically
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

Number the girls 1 (shortest) to 6 (tallest). Each girl must be taller than the girl to her right and the girl in front of her, so heights get **smaller going right** and **smaller going to the front**.

- Girl 6 (tallest) must be at the back left; girl 1 (shortest) at the front right.
- Write each arrangement as (back row) / (front row), left to right:

1. 6 5 4 / 3 2 1
2. 6 5 3 / 4 2 1
3. 6 5 2 / 4 3 1
4. 6 4 3 / 5 2 1
5. 6 4 2 / 5 3 1

(Check one: in #3, back 6 5 2 and front 4 3 1 — each back girl is taller than the one in front: 6>4, 5>3, 2>1 ✓; each row goes down to the right ✓.)

**Answer: 5 arrangements**

solutions.title: Choose the back row
solutions.body:
Girl 6 must be in the back row and girl 1 in the front row. Girl 5 must be either in the back row next to 6, or at the front-left (in front of 6).

- Pick the other two girls of the back row; the front row is whatever is left, sorted tallest to shortest. Then check each back girl is taller than the girl in front.
- Back row choices (with 6) and their front rows:
  - 6 5 4 / 3 2 1 ✓
  - 6 5 3 / 4 2 1 ✓
  - 6 5 2 / 4 3 1 ✓
  - 6 4 3 / 5 2 1 ✓
  - 6 4 2 / 5 3 1 ✓
  - 6 3 2 / 5 4 1 ✗ (3 is not taller than 4 in front)
  - 6 5 1, 6 4 1, 6 3 1, 6 2 1 ✗ (girl 1 can't be in back, nobody is shorter to stand in front of her)
- That leaves 5 arrangements.

**Answer: 5 arrangements**

prompt:
Lou eats 1 jelly bean on September 1st, 3 on September 2nd, 5 on September 3rd, and so on, through the 30 days of the month. Each day he eats 2 more than the day before.

**In all, how many jelly beans does Lou eat in September?**

solutions.title: Look for a pattern
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

| Day | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Eaten that day | 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9 |
| Total so far | 1 | 4 | 9 | 16 | 25 |

The total after $N$ days is $N \times N$ (a square number!). After 30 days the total is $30 \times 30 = 900$.

**Answer: 900 jelly beans**

solutions.title: Pair the days
solutions.body:
- On day 30 Lou eats $1 + 2 \times 29 = 59$ jelly beans.
- Pair the first day with the last: $1 + 59 = 60$. Pair day 2 with day 29: $3 + 57 = 60$. Every pair adds to 60.
- 30 days make 15 pairs: $15 \times 60 = 900$.

**Answer: 900 jelly beans**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2026-27 (from Volume 3, Set 3, Olympiad 2, 2B)

prompt:
Five students sit around a circular table. Their chairs are numbered in order from 1 through 5. Abby sits next to both Ben and Colin. Dalia sits next to both Ben and Sarah. The numbers on Abby's and Colin's chairs add up to 6.

**Who sits in chair number 3?**

solutions.title: Find the seating order first
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Abby is between Ben and Colin: **Colin – Abby – Ben**.
- Dalia is between Ben and Sarah: **Ben – Dalia – Sarah**.
- So around the table: Colin, Abby, Ben, Dalia, Sarah (and Sarah is next to Colin, closing the circle).
- Abby and Colin sit next to each other and their chair numbers add to 6. Next-door chairs around the table are 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-5, 5-1. Only **5 and 1** add to 6.
- If Abby = 1, Colin = 5: Ben = 2, **Dalia = 3**, Sarah = 4.
- If Abby = 5, Colin = 1: Ben = 4, **Dalia = 3**, Sarah = 2.

**Answer: Dalia**

solutions.title: Count steps around the circle
solutions.body:
- Order around the table: Colin, Abby, Ben, Dalia, Sarah.
- Dalia is exactly 2 seats away from Abby, and Sarah/Colin are on the other side.
- Abby and Colin are in chairs 1 and 5 (the only next-door pair adding to 6), which are the two "ends" of the numbering. Moving 2 seats from chair 1 or from chair 5 (away from Colin) always lands in chair 3, the middle chair.

**Answer: Dalia**

prompt: **What is the sum of the digits in this arrangement?** (See the picture.)

solutions.title: Count how many times each digit appears
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

There are sixteen 4s, twelve 3s, eight 2s, four 1s, and one 0.

$$16 \times 4 + 12 \times 3 + 8 \times 2 + 4 \times 1 + 0 = 64 + 36 + 16 + 4 = 120$$

prompt:
Ashley's locker number is a three-digit multiple of 5. The tens digit is the sum of the hundreds digit and the ones digit. The sum of all three digits is 16. No two digits are the same.

**What is Ashley's locker number?**

solutions.title: Find the ones digit first
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- A multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5.
- If it ended in 0, the tens digit would equal the hundreds digit (hundreds + 0). But no two digits are the same, so the ones digit is **5**.
- Then tens = hundreds + 5. Options: 165, 275, 385, 495.
- Digit sums: 12, 14, **16**, 18. Only 385 works.

**Answer: 385**

solutions.title: Use the digit sum
solutions.body:
- Tens = hundreds + ones, so the digit sum = tens + tens = $2 \times$ tens.
- $2 \times \text{tens} = 16$, so the tens digit is **8**.
- Then hundreds + ones = 8, and the ones digit is 0 or 5.
  - Ones = 0 → hundreds = 8, but then two digits are 8. ✗
  - Ones = 5 → hundreds = 3 → **385** ✓

**Answer: 385**

solutions.title: Expanded form
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS Method 1.

Split each number into hundreds, tens and ones:

- Hundreds: $500 + 600 + 700 + 800 + 900 = 3500$
- Tens: $30 + 40 + 50 + 60 + 70 = 250$
- Ones: $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$

$3500 + 250 + 15 = 3765$

**Answer: 3765**

solutions.title: Use the middle number
solutions.body:
- The numbers go up by the same amount each time: $642 - 531 = 111$, $753 - 642 = 111$, and so on.
- So they are evenly spaced around the middle number, 753: $531$ and $975$ average to 753, and so do $642$ and $864$.
- The sum is $5 \times 753 = 3765$.

**Answer: 3765**

prompt: The first 40 odd counting numbers are written. **How many times does '3' appear as a digit?**

solutions.title: Count by place value
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS Method 1.

- The first 40 odd numbers go from 1 to 79.
- '3' in the **tens** place: 31, 33, 35, 37, 39 → 5 times.
- '3' in the **ones** place: 3, 13, 23, 33, 43, 53, 63, 73 → 8 times.
- Total: $5 + 8 = 13$ (33 is counted twice because it has two 3s).

**Answer: 13**

prompt: Ashley has a rectangle made out of paper that is 8 cm by 12 cm. She folds it in half twice, first vertically and then horizontally. The new rectangle looks just like the original rectangle but smaller. **What is the area of the new smaller rectangle in square cm?**

solutions.title: Draw the folded paper
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS Method 1.

- Start: 8 cm by 12 cm.
- Fold the 12 cm side in half: 8 cm by 6 cm.
- Fold the 8 cm side in half: 4 cm by 6 cm.
- Area: $4 \times 6 = 24$ square cm.

**Answer: 24 sq cm**

solutions.title: Halve the area twice
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS Method 2.

- Original area: $8 \times 12 = 96$ square cm.
- Each fold in half cuts the area in half: $96 \div 2 = 48$, then $48 \div 2 = 24$.

**Answer: 24 sq cm**

prompt: In the figure, the whole numbers from 1 through 7 are to be placed, one per square. The sum of the numbers in the left column, the sum of the numbers in the right column, and the sum of the numbers in each diagonal are the same. **What is the least possible product of the numbers across the gray row?**

solutions.title: Try the smallest numbers in the gray row
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- For the smallest product, try putting **1, 2, 3** in the gray row (left, middle, right).
- The left column has 1 plus two more numbers; the right column has 3 plus two more. The columns must have equal sums, so the left column's two extra numbers must add to **2 more** than the right column's two.
- The remaining numbers are 4, 5, 6, 7. Use 5 and 7 (sum 12) on the left and 4 and 6 (sum 10) on the right: both columns add to 13.
- Arrange them so the diagonals (corner – middle 2 – opposite corner) also add to 13:

| 5 | | 4 |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **2** | **3** |
| 7 | | 6 |

Diagonals: $5 + 2 + 6 = 13$ and $4 + 2 + 7 = 13$ ✓

The gray row product is $1 \times 2 \times 3 = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

solutions.title: Why nothing smaller is possible
solutions.body:
- The gray row holds three **different** whole numbers from 1 to 7.
- The smallest product of three different numbers from 1–7 is $1 \times 2 \times 3 = 6$.
- The first method shows an arrangement that really works with 1, 2, 3 in the gray row, so 6 is achievable — and nothing can be smaller.

**Answer: 6**

prompt:
In the following cryptarithm, each different letter represents a different digit in the 6-digit numbers. If $B \neq 0$, **what is the least sum possible?**

```
  BETTER
  BITTER
  BATTER
+ BUTTER
```

solutions.title: Give the smallest digits to the biggest places
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- To make the sum small, start with the hundred-thousands place: B is in all four numbers there, and $B \neq 0$, so **B = 1**.
- E appears in the ten-thousands place (once) **and** in the tens place (four times), so give it the smallest digit left: **E = 0**.
- I, A, U are each in the ten-thousands place once: give them 2, 3, 4 (any order).
- T fills the thousands and hundreds places, R only the ones: **T = 5**, **R = 6**.

$$105506 + 125506 + 135506 + 145506 = 512024$$

**Answer: 512,024**

solutions.title: Add by place value
solutions.body:
Add the columns as "how much each letter is worth":

- Hundred-thousands: $4 \times B$ hundred-thousands → B is worth 400,000 each.
- Ten-thousands: $E + I + A + U$ ten-thousands.
- Thousands and hundreds: $4 \times T$ in each → T is worth 4,400.
- Tens: $4 \times E$ → E is worth another 40.
- Ones: $4 \times R$.

Sum $= 400000B + 10040E + 10000(I + A + U) + 4400T + 4R$.

Smallest choices: B = 1 (B can't be 0), E = 0, $I + A + U = 2 + 3 + 4 = 9$, T = 5, R = 6:

$400000 + 0 + 90000 + 22000 + 24 = 512024$

**Answer: 512,024**

prompt: *(Practice question)* Which of the numbers below is a multiple of 5?

A whole number is a multiple of 5 exactly when its last digit is 0 or 5. Only 55 ends in 5.

solutions.title: Count in fives
solutions.body:
Counting in fives: 45, 50, 55, 60. Of the five numbers, only 55 is on this list.

prompt: *(Practice question)* What fraction of this hexagon is shaded?

solutions.title: Count the triangles
solutions.body:
The hexagon is split into 6 equal triangles and 2 of them are shaded. So the shaded fraction is $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{1}{3}$**

solutions.title: Pair them up
solutions.body:
Group the 6 triangles into 3 pairs. The 2 shaded triangles make one pair out of 3, which is $\frac{1}{3}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{1}{3}$**

prompt:
Three children went home from a party with four balloons each, and four children went home with three balloons each.

How many balloons is that altogether?

solutions.title: Add the two groups
solutions.body:
- Three children with 4 balloons each: $3 \times 4 = 12$.
- Four children with 3 balloons each: $4 \times 3 = 12$.
- Altogether $12 + 12 = 24$.

**Answer: (D) 24**

solutions.title: Notice they are the same
solutions.body:
$3 \times 4$ and $4 \times 3$ are the same number, 12. So the total is $2 \times 12 = 24$.

**Answer: (D) 24**

prompt: How many grams of jam are there in this full jam jar?

solutions.title: Convert kilograms to grams
solutions.body:
The label says 0.4 kg. There are 1000 grams in a kilogram, so $0.4 \times 1000 = 400$ grams.

**Answer: (D) 400 grams**

solutions.title: Use a fraction
solutions.body:
$0.4$ kg is $\frac{4}{10}$ of a kilogram. One tenth of 1000 g is 100 g, so four tenths is 400 g.

**Answer: (D) 400 grams**

prompt:
In one of the five words below, every letter has rotational symmetry.

Which word?

solutions.title: Check each word
solutions.body:
A letter has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after turning it upside down (half a turn). The capital letters that do are H, I, N, O, S, X and Z.
- BISON has B, DOZEN has D and E, SAXON has A, CHINO has C — these letters do not.
- ONION uses only O, N and I, which all do.

**Answer: (A) ONION**

solutions.title: Spot the bad letters
solutions.body:
Turn each word upside down in your head. B, D, E, A and C all change when turned half a turn, which rules out every word except ONION.

**Answer: (A) ONION**

prompt:
Historians say that William the Conqueror was born in 1028.

How many years ago was that? *(The paper was set in 2018.)*

solutions.title: Count on
solutions.body:
From 1028 to 2028 is 1000 years, but 2018 is 10 years before 2028, so it is $1000 - 10 = 990$ years.

**Answer: (D) 990**

prompt: Which of these is closest to 201.8 mm in length?

choices.text: the length of a big toe
the width of one of the pages of this question paper
the distance across a sports stadium
the width of a small galaxy

solutions.title: Change to centimetres

prompt:
The graph shows Pat's journey home from his grandfather's house. On the way he had to return his grandfather's cat and later went back to a bench to read his comic.

How far did he walk altogether?

solutions.title: Add up each part

The graph shows the distance from home. Follow the line:

- back up to 800 m: 200 m
- down to 200 m: 600 m
- back up to 400 m: 200 m
- (flat part: reading, no walking)
- down to 0 m: 400 m

Total: $200 + 200 + 600 + 200 + 400 = 1600$ m.

**Answer: (E) 1600 m**

Going straight home would be 800 m. Twice he walked 200 m back the wrong way and then had to walk those 200 m again. That adds $2 \times 2 \times 200 = 800$ m, so the total is $800 + 800 = 1600$ m.

**Answer: (E) 1600 m**

A match starts at 7.45 p.m. and has two halves of 45 minutes each.

At what time does the match finish?

prompt:

Which of these is most likely to have been her mistake?

choices.text: missing out one of the decimal points

20.18 is a lot smaller than 50.45, a bit less than half of it. Multiplying by 0.4 (which is $\frac{2}{5}$) takes a bit less than half, and $\frac{2}{5}$ of 50 is 20.

prompt:
The sum of the first 5 **odd** positive numbers is 25.

What is the sum of the first 5 **even** positive numbers?

The even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 are each 1 more than the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. So their sum is $25 + 5 \times 1 = 30$.

prompt:
Mr Fussy wants to buy a new house but he does not want a house with the digit 4 in the door number!

The new houses are numbered 1 to 100

How many houses can Mr Fussy choose from?

solutions.title: Count the numbers with a 4
solutions.body:
Numbers with a 4 in the units place: 4, 14, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64, 74, 84, 94 (10 numbers). Numbers 40–49 have a 4 in the tens place: 10 more, but 44 was already counted. So $10 + 10 - 1 = 19$ numbers contain a 4, and $100 - 19 = 81$ are left.

**Answer: (D) 81**

solutions.title: Count the good numbers directly
solutions.body:
Think of 0 to 99 as two-digit numbers 00–99. Each digit can be any of the 9 digits other than 4, giving $9 \times 9 = 81$ numbers. This includes 00 but not 100; 00 is not a house and 100 is a fine house, so the count stays 81.

**Answer: (D) 81**

prompt:
Sam is looking at this block of cubes from one of the five directions shown.

He sees the view below (left).

From which direction is he viewing the block?

solutions.title: Stand on the right
solutions.body:
Picture standing at arrow (C) and looking at the block. The back of the block is then on your right-hand side. The part of the block that is two cubes high is at the back, so you see a row of three squares with one extra square on top at the right-hand end — exactly the view shown.

**Answer: (C) from the right**

solutions.title: Rule the others out
solutions.body:
- From above you see only the top outline of the block, with no heights at all.
- From the front or the back you look across the block's width, and the raised part looks two cubes wide, not one.
- The view from the left is the mirror image of the view from the right, so it has the extra square on the left-hand end; the given view has it on the right.

Only the view from the right is left.

**Answer: (C) from the right**

prompt:
There are roughly three million people who live in Wales.

Nearly six hundred thousand of them speak Welsh.

Approximately what percentage of people living in Wales speak Welsh?

solutions.title: Use 10%
solutions.body:
10% of three million is 300 000. Six hundred thousand is twice that, so it is 20%.

**Answer: (B) 20%**

prompt:
Mo and Jo robbed a bank and stole £100 between them, all in £5 notes.

The amount Mo ran off with was a multiple of £13.

How much money did Jo get away with?

solutions.title: Use both facts about Mo
solutions.body:
Mo's amount is made of £5 notes, so it is a multiple of 5; it is also a multiple of 13. So it is a multiple of $5 \times 13 = 65$. The only such amount up to £100 (that is not £0) is £65, so Jo got $100 - 65 = 35$ pounds.

**Answer: (C) £35**

solutions.title: List multiples of 13
solutions.body:
Multiples of 13 up to 100: 13, 26, 39, 52, 65, 78, 91. Only 65 ends in 0 or 5, so only it can be made from £5 notes. Jo has £35.

**Answer: (C) £35**

prompt:
Fish fingers are made from a block of cod.

The block is cut into 4 bricks, each brick is then cut into 6 planks and there are 4 fingers in each plank.

How many fish fingers does each block of cod make?

solutions.title: Multiply
solutions.body:
Planks: $4 \times 6 = 24$. Fingers: $24 \times 4 = 96$.

**Answer: (E) 96**

solutions.title: Fingers per brick
solutions.body:
Each brick gives $6 \times 4 = 24$ fingers, and 4 bricks give $4 \times 24 = 96$.

**Answer: (E) 96**

prompt:
Because she has square false teeth, my wife makes square bites (with sides of 3 cm) when she eats toast.

What area is left after she takes four bites in a square slice of toast that measures 12 cm × 12 cm?

solutions.title: Take away the bites
solutions.body:
The toast has area $12 \times 12 = 144$ cm². Each bite is $3 \times 3 = 9$ cm², so four bites remove $36$ cm². Left: $144 - 36 = 108$ cm².

**Answer: (B) 108 cm²**

solutions.title: Count 3 cm squares
solutions.body:
Split the toast into 3 cm squares: it is 4 by 4, so 16 squares. Four squares are bitten out, leaving 12 squares of 9 cm² each: $12 \times 9 = 108$ cm².

**Answer: (B) 108 cm²**

prompt:
Teddy buys a cup of coffee and a cake for £3.75, while Freddy buys a cup of coffee and 2 cakes for £6.25.

Each cake costs the same. How much is a cup of coffee?

solutions.title: Find the extra cake
solutions.body:
Freddy's order is Teddy's order plus one extra cake, so a cake costs $£6.25 - £3.75 = £2.50$. Then the coffee costs $£3.75 - £2.50 = £1.25$.

**Answer: (B) £1.25**

solutions.title: Check the options
solutions.body:
If the coffee is £1.25, then the cake is £2.50, and coffee plus 2 cakes is $1.25 + 5.00 = £6.25$. ✓

**Answer: (B) £1.25**

prompt:
The diagram shows a pentagon with its five diagonals drawn in.

How many diagonals can be drawn on a regular hexagon?

solutions.title: Count from each corner
solutions.body:
From each of the 6 corners you can draw a diagonal to every corner except itself and its two neighbours: 3 diagonals. That is $6 \times 3 = 18$, but each diagonal has been counted from both ends, so there are $18 \div 2 = 9$.

**Answer: (B) 9**

solutions.title: Lines minus sides
solutions.body:
Any two of the 6 corners can be joined by a line: $\frac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$ lines. Six of these are sides, so $15 - 6 = 9$ are diagonals.

**Answer: (B) 9**

prompt:
In the Smellie household, Mum changes her socks every day, Dad every other day, Tammy every three days and Timmy every Wednesday.

At the start of this week, Monday 12 November, Mum, Dad and Tammy all changed their socks.

What is the next date all four of the Smellies will change their socks together?

solutions.title: Number the days
solutions.body:
Call 12 November day 0. Dad changes on days 0, 2, 4, …; Tammy on 0, 3, 6, …; so both on multiples of 6: days 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, … Wednesday 14 November is day 2, and Wednesdays are days 2, 9, 16, 23, 30, … The first day on both lists is day 30. November has 30 days, so day 30 is 12 December.

**Answer: (E) 12 December**

solutions.title: Check the dates
solutions.body:
Dad and Tammy change together every 6 days: 18 Nov (Sun), 24 Nov (Sat), 30 Nov (Fri), 6 Dec (Thu), 12 Dec (Wed). The first of these that is a Wednesday is 12 December.

**Answer: (E) 12 December**

prompt:
The diagram shows a square touching three of the sides of a triangle.

What is the total of the shaded angles?

solutions.title: Angles on a straight line
solutions.body:
At each of the three points where the square touches the triangle, the two shaded angles and the square's right angle make a straight line, 180°. So each pair of shaded angles adds to $180° - 90° = 90°$. Three pairs: $3 \times 90° = 270°$.

**Answer: (D) 270°**

solutions.title: Total along the sides
solutions.body:
Along each of the three sides, at the touching point the angles make a straight line: $3 \times 180° = 540°$ in total. The square's three corners that touch the sides take $3 \times 90° = 270°$ of this. The shaded angles are the rest: $540° - 270° = 270°$.

**Answer: (D) 270°**

prompt:
Paige Turner reads twenty pages every morning and half of whatever is left each evening.

How many days will it take Paige to read a book which has 444 pages?

solutions.title: Make a table
solutions.body:
Pages left after each part of the day:
- Day 1: morning $444 - 20 = 424$, evening $424 - 212 = 212$
- Day 2: $212 - 20 = 192$, then $96$
- Day 3: $96 - 20 = 76$, then $38$
- Day 4: $38 - 20 = 18$, then $9$
- Day 5: she reads the last 9 pages in the morning.

**Answer: (C) 5 days**

solutions.title: Work backwards
solutions.body:
She finishes on a morning when 20 or fewer pages are left. At the start of a day, the pages left go 444, 212, 96, 38, 9. On the fifth day only 9 pages remain, which she reads that morning.

**Answer: (C) 5 days**

prompt:
Anna thinks of a number, divides it by 5, adds 20 to it and ends up with the number she first thought of.

What was that number?

solutions.title: Think in fifths
solutions.body:
Dividing by 5 gives one fifth of the number. Adding 20 brings it back up to the whole number, so 20 must be the other four fifths. One fifth is $20 \div 4 = 5$, so the number is $5 \times 5 = 25$.

**Answer: 25**

solutions.title: Try and check
solutions.body:
Try 25: $25 \div 5 = 5$, $5 + 20 = 25$ ✓. (Try 20: $4 + 20 = 24$, too big; try 30: $6 + 20 = 26$, too small — the answer is in between and 25 works.)

**Answer: 25**

prompt:
The diagram shows a floor plan of a house.

The areas of three of the rooms are shown.

Both the bedroom and living room are twice as long as they are wide.

What is the area of the kitchen?

solutions.title: Find the side lengths
solutions.body:
- Bedroom: $18 = 6 \times 3$ with length twice the width, so 6 m long and 3 m wide.
- Living room: $32 = 8 \times 4$, so 8 m long and 4 m wide.
- The study shares the 4 m height of the living room: $20 \div 4 = 5$ m long.
- So the house is $8 + 5 = 13$ m long. The top row is 3 m tall (the bedroom's width), and the bedroom takes 6 m of it.
- Kitchen: $(13 - 6) \times 3 = 7 \times 3 = 21$ m².

**Answer: 21 m²**

solutions.title: Whole house minus rooms
solutions.body:
From the side lengths above the house is 13 m long and $3 + 4 = 7$ m high, so its area is $13 \times 7 = 91$ m². The kitchen is what is left: $91 - 18 - 32 - 20 = 21$ m².

**Answer: 21 m²**

prompt:
A *palindrome*, such as 707 or 2552, is a number that remains the same when read backwards.

What is the largest six-digit palindrome which is a multiple of 6?

solutions.title: Build it from the outside in
solutions.body:
A six-digit palindrome looks like $ABCCBA$.
- A multiple of 6 is even, so the last digit $A$ is even. Make it as big as possible: $A = 8$.
- Next make $B = 9$.
- It must also be a multiple of 3, so the digit sum $8+9+C+C+9+8 = 34 + 2C$ must be a multiple of 3. $C = 9$: 52 no; $C = 8$: 50 no; $C = 7$: 48 yes.

So the number is 897798.

**Answer: 897798**

solutions.title: Check downward
solutions.body:
Palindromes starting with 9 end in 9 and are odd, so none work. Start from 899998 and go down through 89BCCB98-type numbers: 899998 (digit sum 52), 898898 (50), 897798 (48 ✓). $897798 \div 6 = 149633$.

**Answer: 897798**

prompt:
On a ferry, the total number of cars, bikes and lorries is an even number and is less than 100.

The number of cars is one third more than the number of bikes.

The number of bikes is one quarter more than the number of lorries.

How many cars, bikes and lorries are there on the ferry?

solutions.title: Use ratios
solutions.body:
Cars : bikes $= 4 : 3$ and bikes : lorries $= 5 : 4$. Make the bikes match: cars : bikes $= 20 : 15$ and bikes : lorries $= 15 : 12$, so cars : bikes : lorries $= 20 : 15 : 12$. The total is a multiple of $20 + 15 + 12 = 47$. Even and less than 100 means $2 \times 47 = 94$.

**Answer: 94** (40 cars, 30 bikes and 24 lorries)

solutions.title: Start from the lorries
solutions.body:
The lorries must split into quarters, so try multiples of 4. With 12 lorries: bikes $12 + 3 = 15$, cars $15 + 5 = 20$, total 47 (odd). With 24 lorries: 30 bikes, 40 cars, total 94 — even and less than 100. With 36 lorries the total would be 141, too many.

**Answer: 94**

prompt:
Eight friends are sitting around a circular table at Abbie's birthday party.

Abbie has only 3 party-poppers, so she wants to give them to three of her friends, so that no two friends sitting next to each other both get a party-popper.

How many ways are there in which she can do this?

solutions.title: Look at the gaps
solutions.body:
Going round the table, the 5 friends without poppers are split into 3 gaps between the poppers, each gap at least 1. The gaps can be $1, 1, 3$ or $1, 2, 2$ (in some order around the table). Each pattern can be turned round the table into 8 different positions, and no position is repeated. So there are $2 \times 8 = 16$ ways.

**Answer: 16**

solutions.title: Count systematically
solutions.body:
Number the seats 1 to 8. Count the choices that include seat 1: then seats 2 and 8 are out, and we choose 2 non-neighbouring seats from 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 (in a row): $\{3,5\},\{3,6\},\{3,7\},\{4,6\},\{4,7\},\{5,7\}$, which is 6 ways. Each seat is in 6 choices, giving $8 \times 6 = 48$, but each choice has 3 seats and was counted 3 times: $48 \div 3 = 16$.

**Answer: 16**

prompt: *(Practice question)* Which of these shapes has exactly three straight edges?

solutions.title: Count the edges
solutions.body:
- A is a triangle: 3 straight edges.
- B is a circle: no straight edges.
- C is a parallelogram and D is a rectangle: 4 straight edges each.
- E has 2 straight edges and two curved ends.

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Name the shape
solutions.body:
A shape with exactly three straight edges (and nothing curved) is a triangle, and only shape A is a triangle.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: *(Practice question)* What is the value of $20 \times 2$?

solutions.title: Double it
solutions.body:
$20 \times 2$ is double 20, which is 40.

**Answer: (D) 40**

solutions.title: Use tens
solutions.body:
$20 \times 2 = 2 \text{ tens} \times 2 = 4 \text{ tens} = 40$.

**Answer: (D) 40**

prompt:
Harry Potter was born on 31 July 1980.

How many years ago was that? *(The paper was set in November 2020.)*

solutions.title: Subtract
solutions.body:
$2020 - 1980 = 40$, and his birthday in July 2020 had already passed by November.

**Answer: (D) 40**

solutions.title: Count in tens
solutions.body:
1980 → 1990 → 2000 → 2010 → 2020 is four jumps of 10 years, so 40 years.

**Answer: (D) 40**

prompt: Which of the following is closest to the length of my little finger?

solutions.title: Think about real sizes
solutions.body:
- 1 foot is about 30 cm — as long as a ruler.
- 2 km and 4 m are far too long; 3 mm is about the thickness of a coin.
- A little finger is roughly 5 to 7 cm long.

**Answer: (E) 5 cm**

solutions.title: Measure
solutions.body:
Hold a ruler next to your little finger: it reaches about 5 or 6 cm.

**Answer: (E) 5 cm**

prompt: Boastful Grandad says that he can walk 10 miles in 3 minutes. How likely is this?

solutions.title: Work out the speed
solutions.body:
3 minutes is $\frac{1}{20}$ of an hour, so 10 miles in 3 minutes would be $10 \times 20 = 200$ miles per hour — faster than a racing car. Nobody can walk that fast.

**Answer: (A) impossible**

solutions.title: Compare with normal walking
solutions.body:
A person walks one mile in about 20 minutes, so 10 miles takes about 200 minutes — over 3 hours, not 3 minutes.

**Answer: (A) impossible**

prompt:
Chay Pup folds a regular hexagon along each of its diagonals.

The result is the folded triangular shape shown on the right.

When it is unfolded and cut along all of the folds, how many triangular pieces will there be?

solutions.title: Picture the folds
solutions.body:
The folds are the three long diagonals through the centre of the hexagon. They split the regular hexagon into 6 equal equilateral triangles, one for each side.

**Answer: (E) 6**

solutions.title: Count the layers
solutions.body:
The folded shape is one small triangle with all the paper stacked on it. A regular hexagon is made of 6 such triangles meeting at the centre, so cutting along the folds gives 6 pieces.

**Answer: (E) 6**

prompt:
The Simpsons go on their family summer holiday at midday on 22 August and return home at midday on 2 September.

How many nights are they away from home?

solutions.title: List the nights
solutions.body:
August has 31 days. They sleep away on the nights of 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30 and 31 August (10 nights) and 1 September (1 night): 11 nights.

**Answer: (A) 11**

solutions.title: Count days
solutions.body:
From 22 August to 2 September is $(31 - 22) + 2 = 11$ days, and each day of travel from midday to midday includes one night.

**Answer: (A) 11**

prompt:
Spike the hedgehog eats 8 slugs each day except on Sundays, when she eats 10 slugs.

How many slugs does she eat in one week?

solutions.title: Seven eights plus extra
solutions.body:
If she ate 8 every day it would be $7 \times 8 = 56$. On Sunday she eats 2 more, so $56 + 2 = 58$.

**Answer: (B) 58**

prompt:
My baby sister is 1000 days old today.

How many years old will she be on her next birthday?

solutions.title: Count years of days
solutions.body:
One year is 365 days, two years 730 days, three years 1095 days. 1000 days is between 2 and 3 years, so she is 2 now and will be 3 on her next birthday.

**Answer: (A) 3**

solutions.title: Divide
solutions.body:
$1000 \div 365$ is about 2.7, so she is 2 years old and her next birthday will be her third.

**Answer: (A) 3**

prompt:
On each face of a Rubik's Cube the 9 small squares are the same colour, and a different colour is used for each face.

One face has 9 white squares.

How many squares on the surface of the cube are not white?

solutions.title: Count the other faces
solutions.body:
A cube has 6 faces. One is white, so 5 faces are not, each with 9 squares: $5 \times 9 = 45$.

**Answer: (D) 45**

solutions.title: Total minus white
solutions.body:
There are $6 \times 9 = 54$ squares in total, and 9 are white: $54 - 9 = 45$.

**Answer: (D) 45**

prompt:
Postie Patricia delivers letters to all of the **odd**-numbered houses in a street.

If she starts at number 1 and finishes at number 29, how many houses has she visited?

solutions.title: Take away the even ones
solutions.body:
From 1 to 29 there are 29 houses. The even ones are 2, 4, …, 28, which is $28 \div 2 = 14$ houses. So she visits $29 - 14 = 15$.

**Answer: (B) 15**

solutions.title: Pair up
solutions.body:
The odd numbers 1, 3, 5, …, 29: in each ten there are 5 odd numbers (1–10, 11–20, 21–30), and 29 is the last odd number before 30. So $3 \times 5 = 15$.

**Answer: (B) 15**

prompt:
The diagram shows a pentagon with a square placed edge to edge with it. George places another square on each of the other four edges of the pentagon.

How many outside edges does the combined shape now have?

solutions.title: Edges per square
solutions.body:
Each square covers one edge of the pentagon and adds its other 3 edges to the outside. With 5 squares and no pentagon edges left showing, the shape has $5 \times 3 = 15$ edges.

**Answer: (C) 15**

solutions.title: Add and remove
solutions.body:
Pentagon edges: 5. Each square adds 4 edges but hides 1 pentagon edge and its own touching edge: $+4 - 2 = +2$ per square. $5 + 5 \times 2 = 15$.

**Answer: (C) 15**

prompt:
Linus has drawn this pattern on graph paper.

When he continues the same pattern, which of the points A, B, C, D or E will his line go through?

solutions.title: Find the repeating block
solutions.body:
The line climbs diagonally 3 squares, drops straight down, climbs 2, drops, climbs 1, drops — and then repeats. Each block uses 6 squares across. Counting squares from the start, the line is at the bottom at 0, 6, 12, 18, …

Number the columns from the start. The next block runs from column 12: up 3 to column 15, up 2 to column 17, up 1 to column 18. Then it climbs again from the bottom at column 18, reaching height 1 at column 19. Point E is at column 19, height 1. A and B are at height 3 and C and D at height 2 — the line is never there.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Continue the drawing
solutions.body:
Simply carry on drawing the pattern with the dashed line: after the climb of 1 comes a long climb of 3, which starts at the bottom just below C and passes through E one square to the right and one square up.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt:
How many of the numbers in the box below are factors of 2020?

$$2 \qquad 3 \qquad 4 \qquad 5 \qquad 6$$

solutions.title: Test each one
solutions.body:
- 2: 2020 is even ✓
- 3: digit sum $2+0+2+0 = 4$, not a multiple of 3 ✗
- 4: $20$ is a multiple of 4, so 2020 is ✓ ($2020 = 4 \times 505$)
- 5: ends in 0 ✓
- 6: not a multiple of 3, so not of 6 ✗

Three of them.

**Answer: (B) 3**

solutions.title: Break 2020 apart
solutions.body:
$2020 = 4 \times 5 \times 101 = 2 \times 2 \times 5 \times 101$. It has no factor 3, so 3 and 6 fail, while 2, 4 and 5 divide it.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt:
Last week my maths teacher said that today she would be wearing a new scarf. Kiran thought it would be red and plain, Lila suggested blue and stripy, while Manul was sure it would be red and flowery. Each of them was correct in stating **either** the colour **or** the pattern of the scarf.

Which of the following describes my teacher's scarf?

solutions.title: Try the colour
solutions.body:
If the scarf were blue, Kiran and Manul would both be wrong about the colour, so they would both have to be right about the pattern — plain and flowery at once, which is impossible. So the scarf is red. Then Lila is wrong about the colour, so she must be right about the pattern: stripy. Check: Kiran and Manul are right about red. ✓

**Answer: (E) red and stripy**

solutions.title: Check the options
solutions.body:
- Blue and flowery: Kiran gets nothing right ✗
- Plain blue: Manul gets nothing right ✗
- Red and flowery: Lila gets nothing right ✗
- Plain red: Lila gets nothing right ✗
- Red and stripy: Kiran (red), Lila (stripy), Manul (red) ✓

**Answer: (E) red and stripy**

prompt:
I am about to start my day.

In which order should I carry out the following instructions?

- **D** = dry yourself
- **G** = get out of bed
- **P** = put on clothes
- **T** = take a shower
- **W** = wake up

solutions.title: Put the steps in order
solutions.body:
First you wake up (W), then get out of bed (G), take a shower (T), dry yourself (D) and finally put on clothes (P): WGTDP.

**Answer: (D) WGTDP**

solutions.title: Rule out the silly ones
solutions.body:
Waking up must come first, so only A and D are possible. Option A has you putting on clothes before showering. Only D makes sense.

**Answer: (D) WGTDP**

prompt:
Marge Rine has a cube of butter with sides of 4 cm.

She spreads all the butter evenly on her piece of toast which is 8 cm by 10 cm. [Then she adds the jam.]

How thick is the butter on the toast?

solutions.title: Volume divided by area
solutions.body:
The butter's volume is $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$ cm³. The toast's area is $8 \times 10 = 80$ cm². Thickness $= 64 \div 80 = 0.8$ cm $= 8$ mm.

**Answer: (C) 8 mm**

solutions.title: Slice the cube
solutions.body:
The cube covers $4 \times 4 = 16$ cm² to a depth of 4 cm. The toast is $80 \div 16 = 5$ times bigger in area, so the butter is 5 times thinner: $40 \text{ mm} \div 5 = 8$ mm.

**Answer: (C) 8 mm**

prompt:
The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) planted 12 000 trees at Dovestone Reservoir in the Peak District in 32 days, with the help of 15 volunteers.

If all the volunteers worked on their own at the same speed, how many trees on average did each volunteer plant each day?

solutions.title: Divide by both
solutions.body:
Altogether there were $32 \times 15 = 480$ volunteer-days. $12\,000 \div 480 = 25$ trees.

**Answer: (D) 25**

solutions.title: One step at a time
solutions.body:
Each volunteer planted $12\,000 \div 15 = 800$ trees. Over 32 days that is $800 \div 32 = 25$ trees a day.

**Answer: (D) 25**

prompt:
A rectangular piece of paper is folded in half to form a square.

The area of the square is 36 cm².

What is the perimeter of the original rectangle?

solutions.title: Find the sides
solutions.body:
The square has area 36 cm², so its sides are 6 cm. The rectangle is two such squares side by side: 12 cm by 6 cm. Perimeter $= 12 + 6 + 12 + 6 = 36$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 36 cm**

solutions.title: Count square sides
solutions.body:
The rectangle's edge is made of 6 sides of the 6 cm square (2 along each long edge, 1 along each short edge): $6 \times 6 = 36$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 36 cm**

prompt:
The diagram shows **four** overlapping flower shapes.

The areas of the shapes are 4 cm², 9 cm², 16 cm² and 25 cm².

What is the total shaded area in cm²?

solutions.title: Two rings
solutions.body:
The shaded parts are two rings. The outer ring is the 25 cm² flower minus the 16 cm² flower: 9 cm². The inner ring is the 9 cm² flower minus the 4 cm² flower: 5 cm². Total $9 + 5 = 14$ cm².

**Answer: (B) 14**

solutions.title: Alternate signs
solutions.body:
Going inwards, shaded and unshaded parts alternate: $25 - 16 + 9 - 4 = 14$.

**Answer: (B) 14**

prompt:
In 2010 about 120 million digital still cameras were sold worldwide.

By 2018 this number had decreased by 85%.

About how many million digital still cameras were sold in 2018?

solutions.title: What is left
solutions.body:
Decreasing by 85% leaves 15%. 10% of 120 million is 12 million and 5% is 6 million, so 15% is 18 million.

**Answer: (A) 18**

solutions.title: Work out the drop
solutions.body:
85% of 120 is $120 \times 0.85 = 102$. So $120 - 102 = 18$ million were sold.

**Answer: (A) 18**

prompt:
Murben knows that, in some order, the five symbols shown in the picture stand for the numbers five, six, seven, eight and nine in the Cnujian language.

She also knows the four facts shown in the picture.

Which of these Cnujian symbols represents the number 5?

solutions.title: Make a chain
solutions.body:
Call each symbol by its option letter. The facts say: A is greater than E, C is less than D, E is greater than D, and B is greater than C.

The first three give a chain: $A > E > D > C$. The last says $B > C$. So every other symbol is bigger than C, which makes C the smallest number, 5.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Who could be smallest?
solutions.body:
The smallest symbol can never be the bigger one in a fact. A, E and B are each said to be greater than something, and D is greater than C. Only C is never greater than anything, so C is 5.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt:
Marcia thinks of a positive whole number, and puts it into the number machine above:

think of a number → multiply by 3 → subtract 4 → multiply by 5 → add 6 → answer

What is the largest two-digit number that she could obtain as an answer?

solutions.title: Try numbers in order
solutions.body:
- 1: $3 - 4 = -1$, $\times 5 = -5$, $+6 = 1$
- 2: $6 - 4 = 2$, $10$, $16$
- 3: 31
- 4: 46

The answer goes up by 15 each time: 61, 76, 91, 106. So 91 (from 7) is the largest two-digit answer.

**Answer: 91**

solutions.title: Work backwards from 99
solutions.body:
Undo the machine: subtract 6, divide by 5, add 4, divide by 3 — every step must give a whole number. The answer minus 6 must be a multiple of 5, so the answer ends in 1 or 6: try 96: $90 \div 5 = 18$, $18 + 4 = 22$, not a multiple of 3 ✗. Try 91: $85 \div 5 = 17$, $17 + 4 = 21$, $21 \div 3 = 7$ ✓.

**Answer: 91**

prompt:
The numbers 1 to 9 are each placed in one of the squares in the diagram.

The three numbers in each of the two vertical rectangles add up to 9 and 16 respectively, and the five numbers in the horizontal rectangle add up to 25.

What is the total of the numbers in the seven shaded squares?

solutions.title: Spot the double counting
solutions.body:
$1 + 2 + \dots + 9 = 45$. Adding the three rectangles gives $9 + 16 + 25 = 50$, which counts the two unshaded squares (where the rectangles cross) twice. So the unshaded squares add up to $50 - 45 = 5$, and the shaded ones to $45 - 5 = 40$.

**Answer: 40**

solutions.title: Find an example
solutions.body:
Try unshaded squares 1 and 4 (total 5). Left column: 1 plus two numbers making 8, e.g. 2 and 6. Right column: 4 plus two numbers making 12, e.g. 3 and 9. Row: 1 + 4 plus three numbers making 20 from what is left (5, 7, 8): $5 + 7 + 8 = 20$ ✓. The shaded numbers 2, 6, 3, 9, 5, 7, 8 add up to 40.

**Answer: 40**

prompt:
Oranges cost 26p each and lemons cost 30p each.

Gordon spent exactly £5 on a mixture of oranges and lemons.

How many oranges and lemons altogether did he buy?

solutions.title: Use the tens
solutions.body:
£5 = 500p and the lemons cost a multiple of 10p, so the oranges must cost a multiple of 10p too. 26p × (number of oranges) ends in 0 only when the number of oranges is a multiple of 5.
- 5 oranges: 130p, leaving 370p — not a multiple of 30 ✗
- 10 oranges: 260p, leaving 240p = 8 lemons ✓
- 15 oranges: 390p, leaving 110p ✗
- 20 oranges cost more than £5.

So he bought 10 oranges and 8 lemons: 18 fruit.

**Answer: 18**

solutions.title: Count up the lemons
solutions.body:
Try each number of lemons and see if the rest of the 500p divides by 26: 0 lemons leaves 500 (no), 1 → 470, 2 → 440, 3 → 410, 4 → 380, 5 → 350, 6 → 320, 7 → 290, 8 → 260 = 10 × 26 ✓, and larger numbers of lemons (up to 16) give no other solution. So $10 + 8 = 18$.

**Answer: 18**

prompt:
The diagram shows a square and a triangle.

The triangle is formed by a corner and the midpoints of two sides of the square.

The area of the triangle is 150 cm².

What is the perimeter of the square in centimetres?

solutions.title: Fractions of the square
solutions.body:
The three unshaded triangles are $\frac{1}{4}$, $\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{8}$ of the square (the two long ones are half of half the square; the small corner one is half of a quarter). So the shaded triangle is $1 - \frac14 - \frac14 - \frac18 = \frac38$ of the square. Then $\frac18$ is $150 \div 3 = 50$ cm², and the square is $8 \times 50 = 400$ cm². Its side is 20 cm and its perimeter $4 \times 20 = 80$ cm.

**Answer: 80**

solutions.title: Use a side length
solutions.body:
Let the side be $2a$. The three white triangles have areas $\frac12 \times 2a \times a = a^2$, $a^2$ and $\frac12 \times a \times a = \frac{a^2}{2}$. The square is $4a^2$, so the shaded triangle is $4a^2 - 2.5a^2 = 1.5a^2 = 150$, giving $a^2 = 100$, $a = 10$. The side is 20 cm and the perimeter 80 cm.

**Answer: 80**

prompt:
Alun wrote each of the numbers from 1 to 160 on cards and arranged them in 10 rows of 16 cards each.

Bree picked up the cards and arranged them in 16 columns of 10 cards each.

As shown, the cards with the numbers 1 and 160 were in the same place as before. Two other cards were also in the same place as in Alun's arrangement.

What is the smaller of the numbers on these two cards?

solutions.title: Track the differences
solutions.body:
Moving one place to the right, Alun's numbers go up by 1 but Bree's go up by 10, so Bree − Alun grows by 9. Moving one row down, Alun's go up by 16 and Bree's by 1, so the difference shrinks by 15. A card is in the same place when the difference is 0: going $x$ places right and $y$ rows down from the top-left, $9x = 15y$. The smallest solution other than $x = y = 0$ is $x = 5$, $y = 3$ (both give 45). That place is row 4, column 6: Alun's card there is $3 \times 16 + 6 = 54$ (and Bree's is $5 \times 10 + 4 = 54$ ✓).

**Answer: 54**

solutions.title: Write a formula for each
solutions.body:
In row $r$ and column $c$ (counting from 0), Alun's card is $16r + c + 1$ and Bree's is $r + 10c + 1$. These are equal when $15r = 9c$, i.e. $5r = 3c$. So $(r, c) = (0, 0), (3, 5), (6, 10), (9, 15)$, giving the cards 1, 54, 107 and 160. The smaller of the two new ones is 54.

**Answer: 54**

prompt: *(Practice question)* What is the value of $2 + 0 + 2 + 1$?

solutions.title: Ignore the zero
solutions.body:
Adding 0 changes nothing, so it is $2 + 2 + 1 = 5$.

**Answer: (E) 5**

prompt: *(Practice question)* Which of these shapes is **not** a rectangle?

solutions.title: Look for straight sides
solutions.body:
A rectangle has four straight sides and four right angles. Shapes A, B, D and E are rectangles (some are turned or long and thin). Shape C is an oval (ellipse) with no straight sides.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Turning does not matter
solutions.body:
Turning a rectangle round does not stop it being a rectangle, so B and D still count. The only shape with curved edges is C.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt:
I buy 10 plastic dinosaurs at 99p each and give the shopkeeper a £10 note.

How much change should I receive?

solutions.title: Work out the cost
solutions.body:
$10 \times 99\text{p} = 990\text{p} = £9.90$. Change from £10: $£10 - £9.90 = 10\text{p}$.

**Answer: (B) 10p**

solutions.title: Change per dinosaur
solutions.body:
Each dinosaur costs 1p less than £1. Ten of them cost 10p less than £10, so the change is 10p.

**Answer: (B) 10p**

prompt: Which of the following is closest to the length of a car?

solutions.title: Compare with things you know
solutions.body:
A car is about as long as two adults lying head to toe, roughly 4 metres. 40 cm is a toy car; 40 m is longer than a tennis court.

**Answer: (C) 4 m**

solutions.title: Use a parking space
solutions.body:
A parking space is about 5 m long and a car fits in it with a little room left over, so about 4 m.

**Answer: (C) 4 m**

prompt:
An elephant's height is about twice the circumference of one of its feet.

The circumference of one of Nellie's feet is 150 cm.

About how tall is she?

solutions.title: Double it
solutions.body:
Twice 150 cm is 300 cm, which is 3 m.

**Answer: (C) 3 m**

solutions.title: Convert first
solutions.body:
150 cm is 1.5 m, and $2 \times 1.5 = 3$ m.

**Answer: (C) 3 m**

prompt:
Emma decided to paint on her bedroom wall the 11 letters of the word

**MATHEMATICS**

During a school holiday, she painted one letter each day.

She finished on a Friday.

On which day of the week did she paint the first letter?

solutions.title: Count back
solutions.body:
The 11th letter was painted on Friday, so the 1st letter was 10 days earlier. 7 days before Friday is a Friday; 3 more days back is Tuesday.

**Answer: (B) Tuesday**

solutions.title: Count forwards from each option
solutions.body:
Starting on Tuesday: Tue (M), Wed (A), Thu (T), Fri (H), Sat (E), Sun (M), Mon (A), Tue (T), Wed (I), Thu (C), Fri (S) ✓.

**Answer: (B) Tuesday**

prompt:
The pie chart on the right shows the numbers of pupils who answered the question "Is there life in Outer Space?" with a "yes" or "no".

There were 21 pupils who answered "yes".

How many pupils answered "no"?

solutions.title: Read the fractions
solutions.body:
The "no" part is a right angle, a quarter of the circle, so "yes" is three quarters. Three quarters is 21 pupils, so one quarter is $21 \div 3 = 7$.

**Answer: (D) 7**

solutions.title: Compare the parts
solutions.body:
The "yes" part is 3 times as big as the "no" part, so "no" $= 21 \div 3 = 7$.

**Answer: (D) 7**

prompt:
On the first day of this month, the sun rose at Greenwich at 06:54 and set 9 hours and 40 minutes later.

At what time did the sun set?

solutions.title: Add 10 hours, take 20 minutes
solutions.body:
9 hours 40 minutes is 20 minutes less than 10 hours. $06{:}54 + 10$ hours $= 16{:}54$, minus 20 minutes $= 16{:}34$.

**Answer: (C) 16:34**

solutions.title: Add in steps
solutions.body:
$06{:}54 + 9$ hours $= 15{:}54$. Then 6 minutes takes it to 16:00 and 34 more minutes to 16:34 ($6 + 34 = 40$).

**Answer: (C) 16:34**

prompt:
Hannah places a mirror after the word SWIMS like this (see the picture).

What would the reflection look like in the mirror?

solutions.title: Reverse and flip
solutions.body:
In a mirror the word appears in reverse order, S M I W S, and each letter is flipped left-to-right. M, I and W look the same when flipped, but each S becomes a back-to-front S. Option D shows exactly this (and has W and M the right way round).

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Check letter by letter
solutions.body:
The letter nearest the mirror (the last S) appears nearest the mirror in the reflection, so the reflection starts with a back-to-front S, then M, I, W, and ends with a back-to-front S. Options C and E have normal S's, and A and B have the letters in the wrong order.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt:
The shape on the right (shown first in the picture) is rotated 90° clockwise about the point $P$.

Which of the following shows the shape as it now looks?

solutions.title: Follow the triangle
solutions.body:
Before turning, the triangle on top of the white square points up. A quarter turn clockwise makes it point to the right. That rules out A, C and D. The dark square, which was on the upper right of the triangle, turns to end up below the triangle, which is option B.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Turn the paper
solutions.body:
Draw the shape, put your pencil point on $P$ and turn the paper a quarter turn clockwise (like a clock hand going from 12 to 3). The white square stays next to $P$, the triangle now points right and the dark square is underneath it — option B.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt:
Farmer Baar has 36 sheep, some pink and the rest white.

There are twice as many pink sheep as white sheep.

How many of the sheep are pink?

solutions.title: Share into parts
solutions.body:
For every 1 white sheep there are 2 pink ones: 3 parts. One part is $36 \div 3 = 12$, so there are $2 \times 12 = 24$ pink sheep.

**Answer: (D) 24**

solutions.title: Check the options
solutions.body:
If 24 are pink, then 12 are white, and 24 is twice 12 ✓.

**Answer: (D) 24**

prompt:
Sir Pent has a tank with 4 snakes in it.

Slither is twice as long as Monty.

Viper is half as long as Slither.

Rattle is 15 cm long, and half the length of Viper.

How long is Monty?

solutions.title: Work through the snakes
solutions.body:
Rattle is 15 cm and half of Viper, so Viper is 30 cm. Viper is half of Slither, so Slither is 60 cm. Slither is twice Monty, so Monty is 30 cm.

**Answer: (B) 30 cm**

solutions.title: Spot the shortcut
solutions.body:
Slither is twice Monty and also twice Viper, so Monty and Viper are the same length: $2 \times 15 = 30$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 30 cm**

prompt:
Jonathan the tortoise eats 20 g of salad leaves a day.

The leaves are sold in 80 g bags which cost 90p.

How much would it cost to feed Jonathan for 4 weeks?

solutions.title: Days per bag
solutions.body:
One bag lasts $80 \div 20 = 4$ days. Four weeks is 28 days, which needs $28 \div 4 = 7$ bags. $7 \times 90\text{p} = 630\text{p} = £6.30$.

**Answer: (E) £6.30**

solutions.title: Total grams
solutions.body:
In 28 days he eats $28 \times 20 = 560$ g, which is $560 \div 80 = 7$ bags, costing £6.30.

**Answer: (E) £6.30**

prompt:
Pat and Sam like to sit at either end of their sofa, with their three children sitting between them.

In how many ways can they do this?

solutions.title: List the children
solutions.body:
Call the children A, B and C. Their orders in the middle are ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA: 6 ways. For each, Pat can be on the left and Sam on the right, or the other way round: $6 \times 2 = 12$.

**Answer: (B) 12**

solutions.title: Seat by seat
solutions.body:
Left end: 2 choices (Pat or Sam); right end: the other parent. Middle seats: 3 choices, then 2, then 1. Total $2 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 12$.

**Answer: (B) 12**

prompt:
Mr Waddle walks at 2 mph and Mr Ramble walks at 4 mph.

They set off together for a non-stop 12 mile hike.

How long after Mr Ramble finishes does Mr Waddle complete the hike?

solutions.title: Time for each
solutions.body:
Mr Waddle takes $12 \div 2 = 6$ hours and Mr Ramble $12 \div 4 = 3$ hours. The difference is 3 hours.

**Answer: (B) 3 hours**

solutions.title: Where is Mr Waddle?
solutions.body:
When Mr Ramble finishes after 3 hours, Mr Waddle has walked $3 \times 2 = 6$ miles and has 6 miles left, which takes him another 3 hours.

**Answer: (B) 3 hours**

prompt:
I add together three consecutive whole numbers.

Their sum is **always**

solutions.title: Balance around the middle
solutions.body:
The smallest number is 1 less than the middle one and the largest is 1 more. So the three add up to three times the middle number — always a multiple of 3.

**Answer: (E) a multiple of 3**

solutions.title: Try examples
solutions.body:
$1+2+3 = 6$ (even, not a multiple of 5), $2+3+4 = 9$ (odd, not prime), $4+5+6 = 15$. Only "a multiple of 3" is true every time.

**Answer: (E) a multiple of 3**

prompt:
Miss Fitt likes to line her class up in different ways.

When all the pupils are there she can line them up in twos, or in threes or in fives, with nobody left over.

What is the smallest number she could have in her class for that to be true?

solutions.title: Common multiple
solutions.body:
The number must be a multiple of 2, 3 and 5. The smallest is $2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30$.

**Answer: (C) 30**

solutions.title: Check the options
solutions.body:
15 and 45 are odd (not in twos); 20 is not a multiple of 3; 30 and 60 both work, and 30 is smaller.

**Answer: (C) 30**

prompt:
Five girls are sitting around a table.

Each girl makes a "high five" with each of the other girls.

How many "high fives" are made?

solutions.title: One girl at a time
solutions.body:
Ava high-fives the other 4. Bina still has 3 new girls, Clare 2 and Dora 1 (Elph). Total $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$.

**Answer: (A) 10**

solutions.title: Count and halve
solutions.body:
Each of the 5 girls makes 4 high fives: $5 \times 4 = 20$. But each high five involves two girls and was counted twice, so there are $20 \div 2 = 10$.

**Answer: (A) 10**

prompt:
Isaac is 53 years old. His mother is 81.

How many years ago was Isaac's age one third of his mother's age then?

solutions.title: Use the age gap
solutions.body:
The age gap is always $81 - 53 = 28$ years. When his mother was three times his age, the gap was twice Isaac's age, so Isaac was $28 \div 2 = 14$ (and his mother 42). That was $53 - 14 = 39$ years ago.

**Answer: (E) 39**

solutions.title: Test the options
solutions.body:
39 years ago Isaac was $53 - 39 = 14$ and his mother $81 - 39 = 42$, and $14 = \frac{1}{3} \times 42$ ✓.

**Answer: (E) 39**

prompt:
The floor of Milo's rectangular bedroom is completely covered with square carpet tiles.

When he measures the room in tiles, he finds it is 11 tiles long and 8 tiles wide.

How many of the carpet tiles do **not** touch the walls?

solutions.title: Inner rectangle
solutions.body:
Remove the outer ring of tiles: the tiles left form a rectangle $(11 - 2)$ by $(8 - 2)$, that is $9 \times 6 = 54$ tiles.

**Answer: (D) 54**

solutions.title: Total minus edge tiles
solutions.body:
There are $11 \times 8 = 88$ tiles. Edge tiles: $2 \times 11 + 2 \times 8 - 4 = 34$ (the 4 corners were counted twice). $88 - 34 = 54$.

**Answer: (D) 54**

prompt:
Penny has one of each of the coins 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p and 50p. She places each of them inside the shapes on a diagram like the one shown here.

The money in the circle amounts to 61p and the money in the square amounts to 38p.

Which two coins go in the overlapping region?

solutions.title: Find what is counted twice
solutions.body:
All six coins add up to $1 + 2 + 5 + 10 + 20 + 50 = 88$p. The circle and square together give $61 + 38 = 99$p. The extra $99 - 88 = 11$p is the overlap, counted twice. The only two coins making 11p are 10p and 1p.

**Answer: (A) 10p and 1p**

solutions.title: Build it
solutions.body:
The circle needs 61p: $50 + 10 + 1$. The square needs 38p: $20 + 10 + 5 + 2 + 1$. The 10p and 1p are in both, so they go in the overlap, and every coin is used exactly once.

**Answer: (A) 10p and 1p**

prompt:
The large square shown is divided into smaller squares.

What fraction is shaded?

solutions.title: Add the pieces
solutions.body:
The large square is a 4 by 4 grid. The four shaded corner squares are each $\frac{1}{16}$, together $\frac{4}{16} = \frac14$. The middle 2 by 2 block is $\frac14$ of the square and is split into 9 tiny squares, 3 of them shaded: $\frac39 \times \frac14 = \frac{1}{12}$. Total $\frac14 + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{3}{12} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{4}{12} = \frac13$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{1}{3}$**

solutions.title: Measure in tiny squares
solutions.body:
The middle 2 by 2 block of grid squares is made of 9 tiny squares, so one grid square is worth $\frac94$ tiny squares. The whole square (16 grid squares) is worth $16 \times \frac94 = 36$ tiny squares. Shaded: the 4 corners are worth $4 \times \frac94 = 9$, plus 3 tiny squares in the middle: 12 out of 36, which is $\frac13$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{1}{3}$**

prompt:
$JKLM$ is a square.

Another square $PQRS$ touches the midpoint of each of the sides of $JKLM$.

The perimeter of $JKLM$ is 48 cm.

What is the area of triangle $RMS$ in square centimetres?

solutions.title: Fraction of the square
solutions.body:
Each side of $JKLM$ is $48 \div 4 = 12$ cm. Joining the midpoints cuts off four equal corner triangles, which together make half the square, so each is $\frac18$ of it. The square's area is $12 \times 12 = 144$ cm², so triangle $RMS$ is $144 \div 8 = 18$ cm².

**Answer: 18**

solutions.title: Half base times height
solutions.body:
$R$ and $S$ are midpoints, so $MR = MS = 6$ cm and the angle at $M$ is a right angle. Area $= \frac12 \times 6 \times 6 = 18$ cm².

**Answer: 18**

prompt:
The diagram shows a square and a regular hexagon touching a straight line and overlapping.

What is the size of the angle marked $x°$?

solutions.title: Find the triangle under the overlap
solutions.body:
Let $Q$ be the square's corner on the line and $R$ the hexagon's corner on the line, and let $X$ be the point where the square's right edge crosses the hexagon's left edge (the angle $x°$ is at $X$, above the line).
- At $Q$: $180° - 21° - 90° = 69°$ between the line and the square's right edge.
- At $R$: each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°, so $180° - 120° - 21° = 39°$ between the line and the hexagon's left edge.
- In triangle $QRX$ the angle at $X$ is $180° - 69° - 39° = 72°$.
- The angle $x°$ is on a straight line with it: $x = 180 - 72 = 108$.

**Answer: 108°**

solutions.title: Exterior angle
solutions.body:
Using the same triangle $QRX$: the angle $x°$ is the exterior angle at $X$, so it equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: $69° + 39° = 108°$.

**Answer: 108°**

prompt:
More than 60% but less than 65% of the spiders in my cupboard have hairy legs.

What is the smallest number of spiders that could be in my cupboard?

solutions.title: Try each number of spiders
solutions.body:
We need a fraction with that many spiders strictly between 60% and 65%.
- 1 to 5 spiders: possible percentages include 50%, 66.7%, 75%, 60%, 80% — none strictly between 60% and 65%.
- 6: 50%, 66.7% — no. 7: 57%, 71% — no.
- 8: $\frac58 = 62.5\%$ ✓

**Answer: 8**

solutions.title: Think of the gap
solutions.body:
Between 60% and 65% there is a gap of only 5%. The fraction $\frac{k}{n}$ must satisfy $0.6n < k < 0.65n$. For $n = 8$: $4.8 < k < 5.2$, so $k = 5$ works. For each smaller $n$ the interval $(0.6n, 0.65n)$ contains no whole number (e.g. $n = 7$: $4.2$ to $4.55$).

**Answer: 8**

prompt:
Three cats, Flopsie, Lopsie and Topsie, were weighed in pairs.

The weights of each of the three pairs were 5 kg, 8 kg and 9 kg.

What was the weight of the heaviest cat?

solutions.title: Add all the pairs
solutions.body:
Each cat was weighed twice, so $5 + 8 + 9 = 22$ kg is twice the total of the three cats. The three cats weigh 11 kg. The heaviest cat is not in the lightest pair (5 kg), so it weighs $11 - 5 = 6$ kg.

**Answer: 6 kg**

solutions.title: Find each cat
solutions.body:
Total 11 kg. Taking away each pair gives the third cat: $11 - 5 = 6$, $11 - 8 = 3$, $11 - 9 = 2$. Check: $3 + 2 = 5$, $6 + 2 = 8$, $6 + 3 = 9$ ✓. Heaviest: 6 kg.

**Answer: 6 kg**

prompt:
Tabitha writes down a four-digit number $N$.

She then rubs out one of the digits and creates a new three-digit number, $M$, with the three digits that are left (in the same order as before).

The difference between $N$ and $M$ is 2021.

What is Tabitha's original number $N$?

solutions.title: Which digit was rubbed out?
solutions.body:
If she rubbed out any digit except the last, $N$ and $M$ would end in the same digit and $N - M$ would end in 0. But 2021 ends in 1, so she rubbed out the last digit $s$. Then $N = 10M + s$, so $N - M = 9M + s = 2021$. The largest multiple of 9 not more than 2021 is $2016 = 9 \times 224$, leaving $s = 5$. So $M = 224$ and $N = 2245$.

Check: $2245 - 224 = 2021$ ✓

**Answer: 2245**

solutions.title: Estimate, then check
solutions.body:
Taking the last digit off a four-digit number makes it about 10 times smaller, so $N - M$ is about $9M$. Then $M$ is about $2021 \div 9 \approx 224.6$. Try $M = 224$: we need $N = 224 + 2021 = 2245$, and rubbing out its last digit does give 224 ✓.

**Answer: 2245**

prompt: *(Practice question)* Calculate $1 + 10 + 100$.

solutions.title: Use place value
solutions.body:
1 hundred, 1 ten and 1 one make 111.

**Answer: (D) 111**

prompt: *(Practice question)* How many squares are there here?

solutions.title: Check each shape
solutions.body:
The shapes are a triangle, a long rectangle, a slanted parallelogram, a square and another slanted parallelogram. A square needs four equal sides **and** four right angles, so only the fourth shape is a square.

**Answer: (A) 1**

solutions.title: Rule out the look-alikes
solutions.body:
The rectangle has right angles but two sides are longer. The parallelograms have equal-looking sides in places but no right angles. That leaves just one square.

**Answer: (A) 1**

prompt: What is the smallest number of coins which will make 8p?

solutions.title: Use the biggest coins first
solutions.body:
Take the biggest coin that fits: 5p (3p left), then 2p (1p left), then 1p. That is 3 coins: $5 + 2 + 1 = 8$.

**Answer: (A) 3**

solutions.title: Why not 2 coins?
solutions.body:
Two UK coins can make 2p, 3p, 4p, 6p, 7p, 10p, … but never 8p (there is no 3p, 4p or 6p coin to pair with another). So 3 coins is the smallest.

**Answer: (A) 3**

prompt:
It costs 20p to charge my electric scooter which can then travel 25 miles.

How much would it cost if this scooter travelled 100 miles?

solutions.title: Scale up
solutions.body:
100 miles is $4 \times 25$ miles, so it needs 4 charges: $4 \times 20\text{p} = 80\text{p}$.

**Answer: (A) 80p**

solutions.title: Cost per mile
solutions.body:
20p for 25 miles is $\frac{20}{25} = 0.8$p per mile, so 100 miles costs 80p.

**Answer: (A) 80p**

prompt:
Tilly the cat and her 4 kittens each eat 3 cat treats every day.

How many treats altogether do they eat in one day?

solutions.title: Count the cats
solutions.body:
Tilly plus 4 kittens is 5 cats. $5 \times 3 = 15$ treats.

**Answer: (C) 15**

solutions.title: Add up
solutions.body:
Kittens: $4 \times 3 = 12$. Tilly: 3. Total $12 + 3 = 15$.

**Answer: (C) 15**

prompt: Chippy the seagull is flying east. Sadly, he is knocked by another seagull which spins him 180° clockwise. What direction is Chippy now facing?

solutions.title: Half a turn
solutions.body:
180° is half a turn, which always points you in the opposite direction. The opposite of east is west.

**Answer: (E) west**

solutions.title: Two quarter turns
solutions.body:
Clockwise from east: a quarter turn (90°) takes him to south, another quarter turn takes him to west.

**Answer: (E) west**

prompt:
Ringa Bell takes 20 minutes to cycle to school, which is a mile from her home.

What is her average cycling speed?

solutions.title: How far in an hour
solutions.body:
An hour is 3 lots of 20 minutes, so in an hour she would cycle 3 miles: 3 mph.

**Answer: (B) 3 mph**

solutions.title: Speed = distance ÷ time
solutions.body:
20 minutes is $\frac13$ of an hour. $1 \div \frac13 = 3$ miles per hour.

**Answer: (B) 3 mph**

prompt:
This shape, called a sphinx, is made of equilateral triangles, all the same size.

How many of these triangles are needed to make this sphinx?

solutions.title: Draw the triangles
solutions.body:
The base of the sphinx is 3 triangle-sides long. Along the bottom row fit 3 upward and 2 downward triangles (5 in all), and the head on top is 1 more triangle: 6.

**Answer: (C) 6**

solutions.title: Compare areas
solutions.body:
The head is one small triangle. The body is a trapezium which is a triangle of side 3 (9 small triangles) with the top part (a triangle of side 2, 4 small triangles) cut off: $9 - 4 = 5$. Total $5 + 1 = 6$.

**Answer: (C) 6**

prompt:
A Pet Rescue Home has the same number of parrots, cats and dogs.

When the owner of the home looks at all of her pets, she can see 30 legs.

How many cats are there?

solutions.title: Group the animals
solutions.body:
One parrot, one cat and one dog have $2 + 4 + 4 = 10$ legs. 30 legs means 3 such groups, so there are 3 cats.

**Answer: (B) 3**

solutions.title: Check an option
solutions.body:
With 3 of each: parrots $3 \times 2 = 6$, cats $3 \times 4 = 12$, dogs $3 \times 4 = 12$. $6 + 12 + 12 = 30$ ✓.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt:
The spider and the slug love each other. They are 44 cm apart. The spider runs towards the slug at 7 cm/sec and the slug slides towards the spider at 4 cm/sec.

How long is it before they meet?

solutions.title: Closing speed
solutions.body:
Each second the gap shrinks by $7 + 4 = 11$ cm. $44 \div 11 = 4$ seconds.

**Answer: (C) 4 sec**

solutions.title: Second by second
solutions.body:
Gap: 44 → 33 → 22 → 11 → 0 cm. That is 4 seconds.

**Answer: (C) 4 sec**

prompt:
My maths teacher Addum Kwickly has 18 socks (9 pairs of socks).

He puts on clean socks every three days.

How many days can he wear these socks before he has to wash them all?

solutions.title: Days per pair
solutions.body:
Each pair lasts 3 days, and he has 9 pairs: $9 \times 3 = 27$ days.

**Answer: (D) 27**

solutions.title: Careful with socks vs pairs
solutions.body:
He wears 2 socks at a time, so the 18 socks give 9 changes. $9 \times 3 = 27$ days (not $18 \times 3$).

**Answer: (D) 27**

prompt:
In the figure below, the triangles are all equilateral. The dotted line is 12 cm long.

How long in total is the zigzag line?

solutions.title: Two sides per triangle
solutions.body:
Each triangle has its base on the dotted line and its other two sides on the zigzag. In an equilateral triangle those two sides together are twice the base. The bases add up to the dotted line, 12 cm, so the zigzag is $2 \times 12 = 24$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 24 cm**

solutions.title: Imagine equal triangles
solutions.body:
The answer does not depend on the sizes, so pretend there are 4 equal triangles each with a base of 3 cm. Each adds $3 + 3 = 6$ cm of zigzag: $4 \times 6 = 24$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 24 cm**

prompt:
Choco Holic likes packets of Nibletts™.

Which offer gives him the cheapest Nibletts™?

solutions.title: Same price, most packets
solutions.body:
Every offer costs the price of 2 packets. The best one gives the most packets for that money: 5 for the price of 2.

**Answer: (E) 5 for the price of 2**

solutions.title: Price per packet
solutions.body:
If one packet normally costs £1, the offers cost per packet: £2, £1, about 67p, 50p and 40p. The cheapest is 40p.

**Answer: (E) 5 for the price of 2**

prompt:
In this car park problem, cars can only go forwards and backwards.

What is the smallest number of cars that I have to move before I can drive my car straight out of the car park?

solutions.title: Clear the exit row
solutions.body:
The car park is 4 squares wide and 5 deep, and my car is in the middle row on the left. Two upright cars block my row: one in the third column and one in the fourth (next to the exit). Each must leave the middle row completely.
- **Fourth-column car:** above it is another upright car stuck against the top wall, so it must go down one square. That square is taken by the flat car on the bottom row, so first slide the bottom flat car one square left (it can move only that far). Then move the fourth-column car down. (2 cars)
- **Third-column car:** it cannot go down, since the bottom flat car still covers the third column wherever it can be. So it must go up two squares, and those squares are covered by the two flat cars in the top two rows. Slide both of those left one square, then move the third-column car up to the top wall. (3 cars)

That is $2 + 3 = 5$ cars, and each of these moves was forced, so fewer is impossible.

**Answer: (C) 5**

prompt:
The digits of the year 2022 total 6.

How many years will it be until this happens again?

solutions.title: Go year by year
solutions.body:
2023 to 2029 have digit totals 7 to 13. 2030 totals 5 and 2031 totals 6. $2031 - 2022 = 9$ years.

**Answer: (D) 9**

solutions.title: Think about the last two digits
solutions.body:
In 20__, the first two digits give 2, so the last two digits must total 4. After 22 the next two-digit number with digits adding to 4 is 31. $31 - 22 = 9$.

**Answer: (D) 9**

prompt: A snack bar contains 7.5 g of sugar. It is recommended that children aged 10 have at most 24 g of sugar daily. How many of these snack bars could you eat and not exceed this limit?

solutions.title: Count up
solutions.body:
1 bar: 7.5 g, 2 bars: 15 g, 3 bars: 22.5 g, 4 bars: 30 g (too much). So at most 3.

**Answer: (C) 3**

solutions.title: Divide
solutions.body:
$24 \div 7.5 = 3.2$, so 3 whole bars fit within the limit.

**Answer: (C) 3**

prompt: Which is the cheapest price for Seerat's phone contract for a year?

solutions.title: Cost for a whole year

- £26 for 3 months: $4 \times 26 = £104$

- annual: £120

Per month: A $50 \div 6 \approx £8.33$, B $26 \div 3 \approx £8.67$, C £9, D £10, E £9. A is cheapest.
